claim: Language interaction is highly demanding on fast adjustment of speech production.
source: Thus, language interaction is highly demanding on fast adjustment of speech production.
evidence: This is stated as a direct assertion in the abstract based on the nature of language coordination dynamics.

claim: A real-time coupled-oscillators virtual partner (VP) was developed that allows modulation of the ability to synchronise speech with a virtual speaker by changing coupling strength parameters.
source: Here, we developed a real-time coupled-oscillators virtual partner (VP) that allows – by changing the coupling strength parameters – to modulate the ability to synchronise speech with a virtual speaker.
evidence: The authors describe the development of their experimental tool in the abstract.

claim: Intracranial brain activity was recorded from 16 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy while they performed a verbal coordination task with the VP.
source: Then, we recorded the intracranial brain activity of 16 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy while they performed a verbal coordination task with the VP.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of patients and the recording method used.

claim: Patients had to repeat short sentences synchronously with the VP.
source: More precisely, patients had to repeat short sentences synchronously with the VP.
evidence: The task description is explicitly provided in the abstract.

claim: The synchronous speech task is efficient to highlight both the dorsal and ventral language pathways.
source: This synchronous speech task is efficient to highlight both the dorsal and ventral language pathways.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Combining time-resolved verbal coordination and neural activity shows more spatially differentiated patterns and different types of neural sensitivity along the dorsal pathway.
source: Importantly, combining time-resolved verbal coordination and neural activity shows more spatially differentiated patterns and different types of neural sensitivity along the dorsal pathway.
evidence: This is presented as a key finding in the abstract.

claim: High-frequency activity (HFa) in left secondary auditory regions is highly sensitive to verbal coordinative dynamics, while primary regions are not.
source: More precisely, high-frequency activity (HFa) in left secondary auditory regions is highly sensitive to verbal coordinative dynamics, while primary regions are not.
evidence: This is stated as a specific finding in the abstract.

claim: Bilateral engagement was observed in the HFa of the inferior frontal gyrus BA44.
source: Finally, while bilateral engagement was observed in the HFa of the inferior frontal gyrus BA44
evidence: This observation is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: Bilateral engagement in the inferior frontal gyrus BA44 seems to index online coordinative adjustments that are continuously required to compensate deviation from synchronisation.
source: bilateral engagement was observed in the HFa of the inferior frontal gyrus BA44 – which seems to index online coordinative adjustments that are continuously required to compensate deviation from synchronisation
evidence: This interpretation is provided in the abstract based on the observed data.

claim: Interpretation of right hemisphere involvement should be approached cautiously due to relatively sparse electrode coverage.
source: interpretation of right hemisphere involvement should be approached cautiously due to relatively sparse electrode coverage.
evidence: This caveat is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: During conversations, interlocutors tend to imitate each other and align their linguistic representations on several levels including phonetic, syntactic, or semantic.
source: Importantly, analyses of conversational data have highlighted the phenomenon of interactive alignment (Pickering and Garrod, 2004), illustrating that during a verbal exchange interlocutors tend to imitate each other and to align their linguistic representations on several levels including phonetic, syntactic, or semantic (Garrod and Pickering, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Interactive alignment is an unconscious and dynamic phenomenon that possibly renders exchanges between speakers more fluid.
source: This is an unconscious and dynamic phenomenon that possibly renders exchanges between speakers more fluid (Marsh et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Interactive alignment consists of mutual anticipation (prediction) and coordination of speech production, leading to a reduction of turn-taking durations.
source: It consists of mutual anticipation (prediction) and coordination of speech production, leading, for instance, to a reduction of turn-taking durations (Levinson, 2016; Corps et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The synchronous speech paradigm has been overlooked in neuroscience research on coordinative phenomena.
source: However, the synchronous speech paradigm has been overlooked.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the state of the field.

claim: The synchronous speech task is remarkably well performed without any particular training, both between a speaker and a recording as well as between two speakers.
source: Interestingly, this task is remarkably well performed without any particular training, both between a speaker and a recording as well as between two speakers (Cummins, 2002; Cummins, 2003; Assaneo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Synchronous speech favours the emergence of alignment phenomena, such as the fundamental frequency or the syllable onset.
source: Furthermore, synchronous speech favours the emergence of alignment phenomena, such as the fundamental frequency or the syllable onset (Assaneo et al., 2019; Bradshaw and McGettigan, 2021; Bradshaw et al., 2023; Bradshaw et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Delayed/altered auditory feedback tasks can induce speech errors as well as modulations in speech and voice features.
source: These tasks can induce speech errors as well as modulations in speech and voice features (Stuart et al., 2002; Yamamoto and Kawabata, 2014; Karlin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous studies have revealed increased responses in the superior temporal regions compared to normal feedback conditions.
source: Previous studies have revealed increased responses in the superior temporal regions compared to normal feedback conditions (Hirano et al., 1997; Hashimoto and Sakai, 2003; Takaso et al., 2010; Ozker et al., 2022; Floegel et al., 2020; see Meekings and Scott, 2021 for a review of error-monitoring and feedback control in the STG during speech production).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The coordinative behaviour was affected, for both controls and patients, by the coupling parameters of the model with better coordination when the VP was set to synchronise with participants compared to when it was set to speak with a 180° syllabic shift.
source: Overall, the coordinative behaviour was affected, for both controls and patients, by the coupling parameters of the model with a better coordination when the VP was set to synchronise with participants compared to when it was set to speak with a 180° syllabic shift (controls: t ratio = 4.55, p ≤ 0.0001; patients: t ratio = 6.53, p ≤ 0.0001, see boxplots in Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The task produced a rather large coupling variability (controls: range: 0.06–0.84; mean: 0.49; median: 0.49; patients range: 0.11–0.94; mean: 0.55; median: 0.54).
source: This produced, as desired, a rather large coupling variability (controls: range: 0.06–0.84; mean: 0.49; median: 0.49; patients range: 0.11–0.94; mean: 0.55; median: 0.54, see Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by descriptive statistics and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The coordinative behaviour was significantly better than chance for every patient.
source: Nonetheless, while variable, the coordinative behaviour was significantly better than chance for every patient (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Neural responses are present in all six canonical frequency bands, from the delta range (1–4 Hz) up to high-frequency activity (HFa, 70–125 Hz) in the left hemisphere.
source: In the left hemisphere, neural responses are present in all six canonical frequency bands, from the delta range (1–4 Hz) up to high-frequency activity (HFa, 70–125 Hz, see Figure 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A showing neural responses across frequency bands.

claim: Theta, alpha, and beta bands show massive desynchronisation, in particular in the STG BA41/42 (primary auditory cortex), STG BA22 (secondary auditory cortex), and inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) BA44 (Broca's area).
source: More precisely, while theta, alpha, and beta bands show massive desynchronisation, in particular in the STG BA41/42 (primary auditory cortex), STG BA22 (secondary auditory cortex), and inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) BA44 (Broca's area)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The low gamma and HFa bands are dominated by power increase in particular in the auditory cortex (STG BA41/42) and in the IFG BA44.
source: the low gamma and HFa bands are dominated by power increase in particular in the auditory cortex (STG BA41/42) and in the IFG BA44.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The modulation between synchronisation and desynchronisation across frequencies was significant (F(5) = 6.42, p < 0.001).
source: This modulation between synchronisation and desynchronisation across frequencies was significant (F(5) = 6.42, p < 0.001; estimated with linear model using the R function lm).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The whole left hemisphere language network is strongly involved, including both dorsal and ventral pathways.
source: As expected, the whole left hemisphere language network is strongly involved, including both dorsal and ventral pathways (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A.

claim: There is a gradual transition in the direction of correlations as we move up frequency bands, from positive correlations at low frequencies to negative ones at high frequencies (F(5) = 2.68, p = 0.02).
source: The first observation is a gradual transition in the direction of correlations as we move up frequency bands, from positive correlations at low frequencies to negative ones at high frequencies (F(5) = 2.68, p = 0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In the low-frequency bands stronger desynchronisation goes along with weaker verbal coordination, while in the HFa stronger activity is associated with weaker verbal coordination.
source: In other words, while in the low-frequency bands stronger desynchronisation goes along with weaker verbal coordination, in the HFa stronger activity is associated with weaker verbal coordination.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the correlation analysis.

claim: Silhouette scores are systematically higher for behaviour-related activity compared to global activity, indicating greater clustering consistency across frequency bands (t(106) = 7.79, p < 0.001).
source: Indeed, silhouette scores are systematically higher for behaviour-related activity compared to global activity, indicating greater clustering consistency across frequency bands (t(106) = 7.79, p < 0.001, see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Silhouette scores are maximal, in particular for HFa, for five clusters (p < 0.001), located in the IFG BA44, the IPL BA40 and the STG BA41/42 and BA22.
source: Moreover, silhouette scores are maximal, in particular for HFa, for five clusters (p < 0.001), located in the IFG BA44, the IPL BA40 and the STG BA41/42 and BA22 (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: For each frequency band, approximately 2/3 of the channels are only significant in the global activity.
source: Comparing in both hemispheres global activity and behaviour-related activities shows that, for each frequency band, approximately 2/3 of the channels are only significant in the global activity (Figure 3C, orange part).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3C.

claim: There is a dramatic decrease of HFa along the dorsal pathway.
source: Figure 4B (left hemisphere) shows a dramatic decrease of HFa along the dorsal pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Left-STG BA41/42 presents the strongest power increase (compared to baseline) but shows no significant correlation with verbal coordination (t(28) = −1.81, p = 0.08).
source: While left-STG BA41/42 presents the strongest power increase (compared to baseline), it shows no significant correlation with verbal coordination (t(28) = −1.81, p = 0.08; Student's t-test, FDR correction).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The left-STG BA22 shows both a significant power increase in the HFa and a significant negative correlation between HFa and behaviour (t(29) = −4.40, p < 0.0001).
source: By contrast, the left-STG BA22 shows both a significant power increase in the HFa and a significant negative correlation between HFa and behaviour (i.e. VCI) (t(29) = −4.40, p < 0.0001; Student's t-test, FDR correction), marking a fine distinction between primary and secondary auditory cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The brain–behaviour correlation is maximal in the left-IFG BA44 (t(26) = −5.60, p < 0.0001).
source: Finally, the brain–behaviour correlation is maximal in the left-IFG BA44 (t(26) = −5.60, p < 0.0001; Student's t-test, FDR correction).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Both the right STG BA41/42 and STG BA22 present a power increase (compared to baseline) – with a stronger increase for the STG BA41/42 – but neither shows a significant correlation with verbal coordination.
source: However, while both the right STG BA41/42 and STG BA22 present a power increase (compared to baseline) – with a stronger increase for the STG BA41/42 – neither shows a significant correlation with verbal coordination (t(45) = −1.65, p = 0.1; t(8) = −0.67, p = 0.5; Student's t-test, FDR correction).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Results in the right IFG BA44 are similar to the one observed in the left hemisphere with a significant power increase associated with a negative brain–behaviour correlation (t(17) = −3.11, p = 0.01).
source: By contrast, results in the right IFG BA44 are similar to the one observed in the left hemisphere with a significant power increase associated with a negative brain–behaviour correlation (t(17) = −3.11, p = 0.01; Student's t-test, FDR correction).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Coupling is strongest in the auditory regions (STG BA41/42 and STG BA22), but it is also present in the left IPL and IFG.
source: When looking at the analysis of the left hemisphere (Figure 5A), coupling is strongest as expected in the auditory regions (STG BA41/42 and STG BA22), but it is also present in the left IPL and IFG.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The coupling relationship changes when moving along the dorsal pathway: a stronger coupling in the auditory regions with the speech input, no difference between speech and coordination dynamics in the IPL and a stronger coupling for the coordinative dynamics compared to speech signal in the IFG.
source: Notably, when comparing – within the ROI previously described – the PAC with the VP speech and the PAC with the phase difference, the coupling relationship changes when moving along the dorsal pathway: a stronger coupling in the auditory regions with the speech input, no difference between speech and coordination dynamics in the IPL and a stronger coupling for the coordinative dynamics compared to speech signal in the IFG (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The task involving both speech production and perception is efficient to highlight both the dorsal and ventral pathways, from low-frequency activity to HFa.
source: Firstly, the task involving both speech production and perception is efficient to highlight both the dorsal and ventral pathways, from low-frequency activity to HFa (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the discussion.

claim: Spectral profiles of neural responses in the language network are nuanced when combined with behavioural data, highlighting that some regions are involved in the task in a general manner, while others are sensitive to the quality of verbal coordination.
source: Secondly, spectral profiles of neural responses in the language network are nuanced when combined with behavioural data, highlighting the fact that some regions are involved in the task in a general manner, while others are sensitive to the quality of verbal coordination (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the discussion.

claim: The HFa of the IFG BA44 (bilaterally) specifically indexes the online coordinative adjustments that are continuously required to compensate for deviations from synchronisation.
source: Finally, the HFa of the IFG BA44 (bilaterally) specifically indexes the online coordinative adjustments that are continuously required to compensate for deviations from synchronisation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the discussion.

claim: The spatial distinction between primary and secondary auditory regions in terms of their sensitivity to task demands has already been observed in the auditory cortex, particularly in the HFa.
source: This spatial distinction made between primary and secondary auditory regions in terms of their sensitivity to task demands has already been observed in the auditory cortex, particularly in the HFa (Nourski, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Task-dependent modulations in auditory target detection paradigms have been interpreted in terms of selective attention or a bias towards behaviourally relevant stimuli.
source: In these studies, modulations corresponded to increases in activity in response to targets compared to non-targets, which have been interpreted in terms of selective attention or a bias towards behaviourally relevant stimuli (Petkov et al., 2004; Mesgarani and Chang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The observed negative correlation between verbal coordination and HFa in left-STG BA22 suggests a suppression of neural responses as the degree of behavioural synchrony increases.
source: The observed negative correlation between verbal coordination and HFa in left-STG BA22 suggests a suppression of neural responses as the degree of behavioural synchrony increases.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The suppression observed in STG BA22 reflects an SIS-related phenomenon specific to the synchronous speech context.
source: Instead, we propose that the suppression observed here reflects an SIS-related phenomenon specific to the synchronous speech context.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed interpretation.

claim: Suppression of HFa as coordination increases may reflect reduced prediction errors due to closer alignment between perceived and produced speech signals.
source: In our study, suppression of HFa as coordination increases may reflect reduced prediction errors due to closer alignment between perceived and produced speech signals.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed interpretation.

claim: Increased HFa during poor coordination may signify greater mismatch, consistent with prediction error theories.
source: Conversely, increased HFa during poor coordination may signify greater mismatch, consistent with prediction error theories (Houde and Nagarajan, 2011; Friston et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a proposed interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The absence of correlation in the right STG BA22 seems to challenge influential speech production models that propose the right hemisphere is involved in feedback control.
source: Furthermore, the absence of correlation in the right STG BA22 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) seems in the first instance to challenge influential speech production models (e.g. Guenther and Hickok, 2016) propose that the right hemisphere is involved in feedback control.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings in relation to existing models.

claim: The left-lateralised sensitivity to verbal coordination is consistent with works suggesting that both hemispheres are involved depending on the type of error: the right auditory association cortex monitoring preferentially spectral speech features and the left auditory association cortex monitoring preferentially temporal speech features.
source: In this context, the left-lateralised sensitivity to verbal coordination reminds one of the works of Floegel and colleagues (Floegel et al., 2020; Floegel et al., 2023) suggesting that both hemispheres are involved depending on the type of error: the right auditory association cortex monitoring preferentially spectral speech features and the left auditory association cortex monitoring preferentially temporal speech features.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The right temporal lobe seems to be sensitive to speech coordinative behaviour, confirming previous findings using fMRI.
source: Nonetheless, the right temporal lobe seems to be sensitive to speech coordinative behaviour, confirming previous findings using fMRI (Jasmin et al., 2016) and thus showing that the right hemisphere has an important role to play in this type of tasks (e.g. Jasmin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: These findings are in line with the importance of higher-level frontal mechanisms for behavioural flexibility and their role in the hierarchical generative models underlying speech perception and production.
source: These findings are in line with the importance of higher-level frontal mechanisms for behavioural flexibility and their role in the hierarchical generative models underlying speech perception and production (Cope et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: The findings are in line with works redefining the role of Broca's area (BA44 and BA45) in speech production associating it more to speech planning rather than articulation per se.
source: More precisely, they are in line with works redefining the role of Broca's area (BA44 and BA45) in speech production associating it more to speech planning rather than articulation per se (Flinker et al., 2015; Basilakos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Electrodes covering Broca's area show the greatest activity before the onset of articulation and not during speech production.
source: Indeed, electrodes covering Broca's area show the greatest activity before the onset of articulation and not during speech production.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior research.

claim: Broca's area may be a 'functional gate' at a pre-articulatory stage, allowing the phonetic translation before speech articulation.
source: According to these studies, Broca's area may be a 'functional gate' at a pre-articulatory stage, allowing the phonetic translation before speech articulation (Ferpozzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation from prior research.

claim: The synchronous speech task allows to refine the view that Broca's area gates pre-articulatory commands by showing that these pre-articulatory commands are of continuous rather than discrete nature.
source: Our use of a synchronous speech task allows to refine this view by showing that these pre-articulatory commands are of continuous rather than discrete nature.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the current findings.

claim: The discrete (on–off) and ignition-like behaviour of neuronal populations in Broca's area gating pre-articulatory commands before speech may be due to the discrete nature of the tasks used to assess speech production.
source: In other terms, the discrete (on–off) and ignition-like behaviour of neuronal populations in Broca's area gating pre-articulatory commands before speech may be due to the discrete nature of the tasks used to assess speech production.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed interpretation.

claim: The involvement of IFG in accurate speech timing has been previously shown via thermal manipulation.
source: Relatedly, the involvement of IFG in accurate speech timing has been previously shown via thermal manipulation (Long et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: During speech perception, the coupling of theta and gamma bands in the auditory cortex reflects tracking of slow speech fluctuations to spiking gamma.
source: Interestingly, during speech perception, the coupling of theta and gamma bands in the auditory cortex reflects tracking of slow speech fluctuations to spiking gamma (Morillon et al., 2010; Morillon et al., 2012; Hyafil et al., 2015; Lizarazu et al., 2019; Oganian and Chang, 2019; Leonard et al., 2024), similar to what we describe in the auditory cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the IFG, the coupling in the HFa is strongest with the input–output phase difference, a metric that could possibly reflect the amount of error in the internal computation to reach optimal coordination.
source: By contrast, in the IFG, the coupling in the HFa is strongest with the input–output phase difference (input of the VP − output of the speaker), a metric that could possibly reflect the amount of error in the internal computation to reach optimal coordination.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The anatomical connectivity between Broca's and Wernicke's territory via the long segment of the arcuate fasciculus possibly sets the base for a mapping from speech representations in Wernicke's area to the predictive proprioceptive adjustments processed in Broca's area.
source: This well fits with the anatomical connectivity that has been described between Broca's and Wernicke's territory via the long segment of the arcuate fasciculus, possibly setting the base for a mapping from speech representations in Wernicke's area to the predictive proprioceptive adjustments processed in Broca's area (Catani and ffytche, 2005; Oestreich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The findings align with broader theories on the relationship between perception and action, such as predictive coding and active inference, which propose shared sensory prediction mechanism and neural computational architecture for both processes.
source: This also aligns with broader theories on the relationship between perception and action, such as predictive coding and active inference, which propose shared sensory prediction mechanism and neural computational architecture for both processes (Friston et al., 2017; Friston et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Models describing language interaction consider that listeners covertly imitate the speaker's speech and timely construct a representation of the underlying communicative intention which allows early fluent turn-taking.
source: Finally, while the case of synchronous speech may seem quite far away from real-life conversational contexts, the models describing language interaction consider that listeners covertly imitate the speaker's speech and timely construct a representation of the underlying communicative intention which allows early fluent turn-taking (Pickering and Gambi, 2018; Levinson, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ability to synchronise in spontaneous speech synchronisation correlates to the degree of lateralisation of the arcuate fasciculus, with high synchronisers showing greater lateralisation to the left than low synchronisers.
source: Importantly, the ability to synchronise correlates to the degree of lateralisation of the arcuate fasciculus, that connects the IFG and the auditory temporal regions, high synchronisers showing greater lateralisation to the left than the low synchronisers.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior research (Assaneo et al., 2019).

claim: The more the structural connectivity of the arcuate fasciculus is lateralised in the left hemisphere, the more the activity of the IFG is synchronised with the envelope of the audio stimulus during a passive listening task.
source: The more this structural connectivity of the arcuate fasciculus is lateralised in the left hemisphere, the more the activity of the IFG is synchronised with the envelope of the audio stimulus of the SSS test, during a passive listening task.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior research (Assaneo et al., 2019).

claim: Thirty participants (17 women, mean age 24.7 years, range 19–42 years) took part in the control study.
source: Thirty participants (17 women, mean age 24.7 years, range 19–42 years) took part in the study.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Five control participants (two women) were excluded from analysis for poor signal-to-noise ratio in speech recordings.
source: Five participants (two women) were excluded from analysis for poor signal-to-noise ratio in speech recordings.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Sixteen patients (seven women, mean age 29.8 years, range 17–50 years) with pharmacoresistant epilepsy took part in the study.
source: Sixteen patients (seven women, mean age 29.8 years, range 17–50 years) with pharmacoresistant epilepsy took part in the study.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: In none of the patients were the auditory areas part of their epileptogenic zone as identified by experienced epileptologists.
source: In none of them were the auditory areas part of their epileptogenic zone as identified by experienced epileptologists.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The sEEG signal was recorded using depth electrodes shafts with a 0.8-mm diameter containing 5–18 electrode contacts.
source: The sEEG signal was recorded using depth electrodes shafts with a 0.8-mm diameter containing 5–18 electrode contacts (Dixi Medical or Alcis, Besançon, France).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Sixteen patients with a total of 236 electrodes (145 in the left hemisphere) and 2395 contacts (1459 in the left hemisphere) were recorded.
source: Sixteen patients with a total of 236 electrodes (145 in the left hemisphere) and 2395 contacts (1459 in the left hemisphere, see Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Four stimuli consisted of four sentences: 'papi mamie', 'papi m'a dit', 'mamie lavait ma main', and 'mamie manie ma main'.
source: Stimuli consisted of four sentences: 'papi mamie' (/papi mami/, grandpa grandma)/'papi m'a dit' (/papi ma di/, grandpa told me)/'mamie lavait ma main' (/mami lavɛ ma mɛ̃/, grandma washed my hand)/'mamie manie ma main' (/mami mani ma mɛ̃/, grandma handles my hand).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The four sentences purposely differed in terms of number of syllables (4-4-6-6).
source: The four sentences purposely differed in terms of number of syllables (4-4-6-6).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Sentence durations were 2.07, 2.11, 3.16, and 2.87 s, respectively, with a syllable rate of ~3 Hz.
source: Sentence durations were 2.07, 2.11, 3.16, and 2.87 s, respectively, with a syllable rate of ~3 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The experiment consisted of 24 trials (14 s long, speech rate ~3 Hz, yielding ~1000 syllables).
source: This was identical to the training but consisted of 24 trials (14 s long, speech rate ~3 Hz, yielding ~1000 syllables).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: For a third of the trials, the VP had a neutral behaviour (close to zero coupling: k = ±0.01).
source: More precisely, for a third of the trials, the VP had a neutral behaviour (close to zero coupling: k = ±0.01).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: For a third of the trials, the VP had a moderate coupling, meaning that the VP synchronised more to the participant speech (k = −0.09).
source: For a third, it had a moderate coupling, meaning that the VP synchronised more to the participant speech (k = −0.09).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: For the last third of the trials, the VP had a moderate coupling but with a phase shift of π/2, meaning that it moderately aimed to speak in between the participant syllables (k = +0.09).
source: And for the last third of the trials, the VP had a moderate coupling but with a phase shift of π/2, meaning that it moderately aimed to speak in between the participant syllables (k = +0.09).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Depending on patient fatigue, a second experimental session with 24 extra trials was proposed (for 6 of the 16 patients).
source: Depending on patient fatigue, a second experimental session with 24 extra trials was proposed (for 6 of the 16 patients).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The control group participant runs a single session of 48 trials.
source: The control group participant runs a single session of 48 trials.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The VP environment is built upon the Psychtoolbox-3 programme and operates within MATLAB, leveraging custom C subroutines to boost its performance.
source: The VP environment is built upon the Psychtoolbox-3 programme and operates within MATLAB, leveraging custom C subroutines to boost its performance.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The VP operation revolves around a loop whose iterations are executed at consistent intervals of Δt = 4 ms.
source: Its operation revolves around a loop whose iterations are executed at consistent intervals of Δt = 4 ms.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Speech signals of the participants and the VP were downsampled from 48 to 16 kHz.
source: Firstly, raw speech signals were downsampled from 48 to 16 kHz.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Speech envelope was extracted using a pass-band filter between 2.25 and 5 Hz.
source: Then speech envelope was extracted using a pass-band filter between 2.25 and 5 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The signal was offline re-referenced using bipolar montage to increase spatial sensitivity and reduce passive volume conduction from neighbouring regions.
source: To increase spatial sensitivity and reduce passive volume conduction from neighbouring regions (Mercier et al., 2017), the signal was offline re-referenced using bipolar montage.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section with a citation.

claim: Channels with a variance greater than 2*IQR were tagged as artefacted channels (6% of the channels).
source: Channels with a variance greater than 2*IQR (interquartile range, i.e. a non-parametric estimate of the standard deviation) were tagged as artefacted channels (6% of the channels).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Six canonical frequency bands were investigated: delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), low gamma (30–50 Hz), and HFa (70–125 Hz).
source: Six canonical frequency bands were investigated by averaging the power spectra between their respective boundaries: delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), low gamma (30–50 Hz), and HFa (70–125 Hz).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.
